q-64333.name: Question 1
q-64333.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-2\,j+2\,k)\times (6\,i-4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-6+8)i-(3-12)j+(-4+12)k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+8\,k.\end{aligned}
$$
